instructional_purpose: Introduces the closed set of free-standing personal pronouns and establishes the principle that a word with no case endings can still occupy a case-bearing slot. It also fixes the division of labour between free pronouns and suffixed ones.
concepts_taught: inventory of free-standing personal pronouns
person, gender and number contrasts inside the pronoun set
gender syncretism in the dual
fixed form (مبني) versus occupied case slot (محل)
free pronoun as clause-initial topic
free pronoun in the predicate slot for emphasis
distributional split between free and suffixed pronoun series

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The free personal pronoun series is closed and invariant: no member changes shape for case.
A form that never inflects can still be assigned a case value by the slot it fills, so analysis must record a positional case instead of a surface ending.
Dual reference neutralises gender: one second-person dual and one third-person dual form cover both genders.
The lesson counts the inventory at twelve and presents it as complete; the separate accusative free-pronoun series built on the base إيّا is never introduced.

A free pronoun standing after a finite verb is labelled an emphatic subject; the mainstream account treats it as a reinforcing appositive to a subject already carried by the verb, not as a second subject.

A bare free pronoun is offered as a predicate of a definite topic; that pattern normally needs a separating-pronoun or contrastive context, so the isolated illustration should be reviewed before being projected onto real text.

recognition_criteria: the word stands alone as an orthographic unit and is not welded to a preceding host
it carries person reference without any lexical content
its shape is identical wherever it appears in the clause, so case must be read off the slot
position before a nominal predicate signals topic use; position after a complete verbal clause signals reinforcement
procedures: read person, gender and number directly off the pronoun's shape
determine the slot the pronoun sits in (topic, predicate, post-verbal reinforcement)
state that the form is fixed, then name the case value the slot confers and the function label
when choosing between series, ask whether the pronoun is first in its clause or needs prominence: if so take the free form, otherwise take the suffixed form
conditions: free form is required when the pronoun opens the clause
free form is used when prominence or contrast is wanted
suffixed form is required after a verb, a noun, or a governing particle
exceptions: dual forms do not distinguish gender, unlike singular and plural
fixed form does not mean absence of case: a positional case is still assigned
contrasts: free versus suffixed pronoun for the same referent
topic use versus predicate use of the same pronoun shape
masculine versus feminine second-person singular, and masculine versus feminine plural, which differ only by a final vowel or gemination

common_mistakes.pattern: placing a free pronoun in a slot that only accepts a suffixed one, for instance directly after a transitive verb
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the object position is filled by an attached form; a free pronoun there leaves the verb without a licensed complement
common_mistakes.correction_principle: select the series by host: verb, noun and particle hosts take the attached series

common_mistakes.pattern: ignoring the vowel that separates the two second-person singular forms
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the addressee's gender is carried entirely by that final vowel, so dropping it destroys the reference
common_mistakes.correction_principle: treat the final short vowel of the second-person singular as meaning-bearing, not decorative

common_mistakes.pattern: interchanging the two third-person plural forms
common_mistakes.why_wrong: one is used for all-female groups only, the other for male or mixed groups, so the swap misidentifies the referent set
common_mistakes.correction_principle: check the composition of the referent group before choosing the plural form

misleading_shortcuts: treating 'indeclinable' as 'has no case', which blocks any later analysis that needs a case value
assuming the twelve listed forms exhaust the pronoun system, which hides the accusative free series
assuming a free pronoun before a noun always means a topic-comment reading
worked_analysis_stages: name the word class of the pronoun
state that its form is fixed
name the case value conferred by its position
name the grammatical function label attached to that position
paradigms: a person-by-number grid of free pronouns covering singular, dual and plural for first, second and third person, with second and third person split by gender
a reduced singular/plural version of the same grid reused as a completion exercise
exercise_types: multiple-choice form identification
multiple-choice function identification
short translation into Arabic
fill-in series requiring the correct pronoun
paradigm completion
end-of-lesson quiz combining recall, function labelling and positional-case questions
prerequisite_knowledge: topic-comment structure of the verbless sentence
the case labels and what they mark
gender and number marking on nouns and adjectives
new_knowledge: the complete free pronoun inventory as a closed class
the doctrine of positional case for invariant words
the series-selection rule between free and attached pronouns
later_dependencies: sentences headed by copular and other governing operators
sarf_relevance: low — the forms are listed as an inventory, not derived by any root-and-pattern process
nahw_relevance: high — every member is given a syntactic function and a positional case, which is core clause analysis
tutor_drill_relevance: high for controlled substitution drills: person/gender/number selection and series selection are both objectively checkable
rich_hover_relevance: high — a hover on any of these forms needs person, gender, number, invariance, and the positional case of the current slot
corpus_pvn_relevance: n-kind entries: the free personal pronouns are traditionally classed as invariant nouns, so they belong with noun-class headwords carrying an invariance flag; no v-kind or p-kind entries arise from this lesson
required_evidence: per occurrence, the surrounding clause is needed: whether a verb precedes, whether a nominal predicate follows, and whether contrast is intended. The form alone fixes person, gender and number but never fixes function or case value.
uncertainty_flags: rival analyses: post-verbal free pronoun as emphatic subject versus reinforcing appositive
the predicate-slot illustration is unusual enough to need review before automatic projection
inventory presented as complete while the accusative free series is omitted

instructional_purpose: Teaches the attached pronoun series and the three host categories that license it, so that a suffix can be read correctly as an object, a possessor, or the complement of a governing particle. It also introduces the conditioned shape changes inside that series.
concepts_taught: inventory of attached pronoun suffixes
host category decides the suffix's role
possessor suffix on a noun
object suffix on a verb
pronoun complement after a governing particle
two shapes of the first-person singular suffix
protective nūn before the first-person suffix on verbs
vowel harmony in the third-person h-series after a front vowel or glide
loss of nunation on a host carrying a possessor suffix

linguistic_propositions.proposition: An attached pronoun is not an independent word; it is licensed only by a host and inherits its role from that host's category.
The same suffix shape can be an object on a verb and a possessor on a noun, so the host category, not the suffix, disambiguates the role.
The first-person singular suffix appears bare after nouns and governing particles but is preceded by a protective nūn after verbs.
The third-person h-series takes a front vowel when the preceding segment is a kasra or a yāʾ.
The lesson explains loss of nunation by saying the structure resembles an annexation; the standard analysis is that it is an annexation, with the suffix as the dependent term.
The protective nūn is presented as a verb-only phenomenon; it also occurs with certain governing particles, which the lesson does not mention.
A free accusative pronoun built on the base إيّا surfaces in one answer key without being taught anywhere in the lesson, so that item cannot be treated as delivered content.
A suffix after a governing particle is described as sitting in the genitive position, which requires the learner to accept positional case on an invariant form.

recognition_criteria: the pronoun has no independent orthographic word boundary and closes out its host
identify the host first: a finite verb, a noun, or a governing particle
a protective nūn immediately before a first-person suffix signals a verbal host
a front vowel on the h-series signals a preceding kasra or glide, not a different pronoun
absence of nunation on a noun that also carries a person suffix signals the annexation reading
procedures: segment the word into host plus suffix
classify the host category
assign the suffix's role from that category: complement of a verb, possessor of a noun, or complement of a particle
select the correct allomorph of the first-person suffix according to whether the host is verbal
apply the front-vowel harmony rule to the h-series when the preceding segment requires it
state the positional case matching the assigned role
conditions: object reading requires a verbal host
possessor reading requires a nominal host
genitive-position reading requires a governing particle host
the protective nūn is inserted only before the first-person singular suffix on the relevant hosts
harmony on the h-series is triggered by a preceding front vowel or glide
exceptions: the first-person singular is the only person with two distinct shapes conditioned by host type
the h-series is the only sub-series whose vowel is conditioned by the preceding segment
contrasts: object suffix versus possessor suffix with identical surface shape
bare first-person suffix versus the shape with protective nūn
back-vowel versus front-vowel realisation of the h-series
attached series versus the free series taught in the previous lesson

common_mistakes.pattern: attaching the bare first-person suffix directly to a verb without the protective nūn
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the resulting form is read as a possessive on a nominal, so the intended object reading is lost
common_mistakes.correction_principle: insert the protective nūn whenever the first-person singular suffix follows a verbal host

common_mistakes.pattern: keeping the back vowel on the h-series after a preceding front vowel
common_mistakes.why_wrong: it violates the conditioned harmony and produces a shape that does not occur
common_mistakes.correction_principle: let the preceding segment determine the vowel of the h-series

common_mistakes.pattern: using a free pronoun where the host requires an attached one
common_mistakes.why_wrong: a verb, noun or governing particle cannot take a free pronoun as its complement
common_mistakes.correction_principle: choose the series from the host category before choosing the person form

misleading_shortcuts: reading a suffix's role off the suffix itself rather than off the host, which collapses object and possessor
treating the h-series vowel alternation as two different pronouns
assuming the protective nūn is a purely verbal device with no other environments
assuming a one-to-one mapping between English possessives and Arabic person suffixes without checking the host
worked_analysis_stages: split host from suffix
name the host category
name the suffix's function
give the positional case implied by that function
paradigms: a two-column series chart contrasting the shapes used after a verb with those used after a noun or governing particle, across all persons
a single-noun host paradigm cycled through the person suffixes as a completion exercise
exercise_types: multiple-choice meaning identification
multiple-choice rule justification for the conditioned vowel
short translation into Arabic
fill-in series with the correct suffix
paradigm completion over one nominal host
end-of-lesson quiz mixing form recall, terminology and role labelling
prerequisite_knowledge: the free pronoun inventory and its person/gender/number contrasts
annexation and definiteness effects on a noun
the fact that governing particles impose the genitive
basic past-tense verb shapes
reuses_from_earlier: L1.M5.01 free pronoun inventory and the free/attached distribution rule
new_knowledge: the attached suffix inventory with its host-conditioned two-column split
the protective nūn as a conditioning device
front-vowel harmony in the h-series
the mapping from host category to pronoun role
later_dependencies: object marking and clause complement structure
pronoun complements of the operators that govern nominal sentences
sarf_relevance: high — clitic segmentation, allomorph selection and a conditioned vowel alternation are all word-form decisions
nahw_relevance: high — the same suffix receives different functions and positional cases depending on its host
tutor_drill_relevance: high — host-to-role mapping and allomorph selection are both mechanically checkable in drills
rich_hover_relevance: high — a hover on a suffixed word must expose the host/suffix split, the person values, the role, and the positional case
corpus_pvn_relevance: n-kind and v-kind hosts both carry these suffixes, and p-kind governing particles do too, so the entries needed are the host lexemes plus a clitic-segmentation layer; the suffixes themselves are best held as an affix inventory rather than as standalone headwords
required_evidence: per occurrence, the host must be categorised (verb, noun, or governing particle) and the immediately preceding segment inspected for the harmony trigger. Role and positional case cannot be inferred from the suffix shape alone.
uncertainty_flags: nunation loss framed as annexation-like rather than as annexation proper
protective nūn scope understated relative to standard descriptions
an untaught free accusative pronoun appears only in an answer key

proposed_new_units.summary: A decision table that maps a pronominal clitic plus its host category to a single role reading (verbal complement, possessor in annexation, or complement of a governing particle) together with the positional case that follows.
proposed_new_units.why_existing_insufficient: u-s09 covers the layering of clitics onto stems and u-n03 covers governance in general, but neither provides the host-category-to-role decision that a per-occurrence annotator needs when the same suffix shape is ambiguous between object and possessor.

instructional_purpose: Introduces the demonstrative words as a class organised by proximity, gender and number, and teaches how the definiteness of the following noun decides whether the result is a phrase or a complete sentence.
concepts_taught: demonstrative inventory split by near and far reference
gender agreement of the demonstrative with its target
number agreement including dual and plural forms
the definiteness requirement on a noun modified by a demonstrative
phrase reading versus sentence reading depending on the article
non-rational plurals taking a feminine singular demonstrative
demonstratives as topic, as modifier, and as predicate
invariance of most demonstratives against the declinable duals

linguistic_propositions.proposition: Demonstratives are organised on a proximity axis, with distinct near and far series.
A demonstrative agrees with its target in gender and number, and the plural human forms are distinct from the singular ones.
When a demonstrative precedes a noun bearing the definite article, the sequence is a phrase; when the noun is indefinite, the same sequence is a complete verbless sentence.
Plurals of non-rational referents take the feminine singular demonstrative rather than a human plural form.

The lesson labels the definite noun after a demonstrative a modified noun, that is, it treats the demonstrative as a modifier; the standard analysis makes the demonstrative the head of its slot and the following definite noun an appositive to it.
The dual demonstratives are declared declinable while the rest of the class is declared invariant.
Proximity is said to be decided by perceived distance, physical or figurative, which is a usage heuristic rather than a formal rule that a parser can apply.
The class is presented as a two-way near/far opposition; the intermediate-distance member of the series is not introduced.

recognition_criteria: a closed-class pointing word occupying a nominal slot
gender and number of the demonstrative match the referent, so mismatch signals a different target
presence of the definite article on the next word signals a phrase reading; its absence signals a predication
a human plural referent licenses the plural demonstratives; a non-rational plural does not
procedures: identify the referent's gender, number and rationality
choose near or far according to the intended distance
select the matching demonstrative from the grid
check the following noun for the definite article to control whether a phrase or a sentence results
for duals, apply dual declension rather than treating the form as invariant
state the positional case for the invariant members
conditions: a phrase reading requires the definite article on the noun that follows
human plural demonstratives require rational plural referents
dual demonstratives require a dual referent and then vary with case
exceptions: dual demonstratives are declinable while the rest of the class is not
non-rational plurals break number agreement by taking a feminine singular demonstrative
contrasts: near versus far series
masculine versus feminine within each distance
phrase reading versus sentence reading of the same word sequence
human plural demonstrative versus feminine singular demonstrative for non-rational plurals
invariant members versus declinable dual members

common_mistakes.pattern: omitting the definite article on the noun after a demonstrative when a phrase was intended
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the sequence is then parsed as a complete predication, which changes the utterance from a noun phrase into a statement
common_mistakes.correction_principle: the article is the switch between phrase and sentence, so set it deliberately according to the intended reading

common_mistakes.pattern: pairing a masculine demonstrative with a feminine noun
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the demonstrative must agree with its target, so a mismatch points at a different referent or is simply ungrammatical
common_mistakes.correction_principle: read gender off the target noun before selecting the demonstrative

common_mistakes.pattern: using a human plural demonstrative for a plural of things
common_mistakes.why_wrong: non-rational plurals are treated as feminine singular for agreement purposes
common_mistakes.correction_principle: check rationality of the plural referent before choosing between the human plural form and the feminine singular form

misleading_shortcuts: treating the demonstrative as an adjective, which then predicts adjective-like agreement and ordering
assuming number agreement is uniform and so extending human plural forms to plurals of things
treating the whole class as invariant and missing the dual declension
reading the near/far choice as purely physical distance
worked_analysis_stages: name the word class
state that the form is fixed, where it is
name the positional case conferred by the slot
name the function label for that slot
paradigms: a proximity-by-gender grid spanning near and far, singular, dual and plural
a reduced version of the same grid used as a completion exercise
a structural table showing demonstrative plus article plus noun as a fixed template
exercise_types: multiple-choice form selection
multiple-choice meaning discrimination between phrase and sentence readings
short translation into Arabic
fill-in series with the correct demonstrative
paradigm completion
end-of-lesson quiz mixing agreement, definiteness and positional case
prerequisite_knowledge: the definite article and its effect on definiteness
gender marking on nouns
verbless sentence structure
the case labels and the notion of positional case
reuses_from_earlier: positional case for invariant words, established in L1.M5.01
new_knowledge: the demonstrative inventory organised by proximity
the definiteness switch between phrase and sentence readings
the rationality-sensitive agreement rule for plurals
declinable duals as an exception inside an otherwise invariant class
later_dependencies: relative clauses, whose heads are often demonstrative-marked
definiteness agreement in later noun-phrase syntax
anaphora and reference tracking in connected text
sarf_relevance: low — the members are memorised shapes, with only the duals showing an inflectional alternation
nahw_relevance: high — definiteness licensing, agreement and positional case all sit in clause syntax
tutor_drill_relevance: high — agreement selection and the article switch produce unambiguous right/wrong drill items
rich_hover_relevance: high — a hover must state proximity, gender, number, invariance or dual inflection, and whether the following noun is in an appositive relation
corpus_pvn_relevance: n-kind entries: demonstratives are classed as nouns in the traditional taxonomy, so they need noun-class headwords with proximity and agreement features plus an invariance flag; the dual members additionally need inflected surface forms
required_evidence: per occurrence, the following word must be inspected for the definite article, the referent's gender, number and rationality must be recoverable, and for duals the case-bearing context must be known.
uncertainty_flags: school-dependent: whether the dual demonstratives are genuinely declinable or invariant with substituted endings
rival analyses: demonstrative as modifier of the following noun versus demonstrative as head with the noun in apposition
the intermediate-distance member of the series is absent from the presented inventory

proposed_new_units.summary: A licensing table keyed on demonstrative plus following nominal that returns the phrase reading when the nominal is definite and the predication reading when it is indefinite, together with the agreement conditions (gender, number, rationality) that must hold for each.
proposed_new_units.why_existing_insufficient: u-n10 covers attachment and referent resolution and u-n09 covers positional case, but neither encodes the definiteness switch that decides whether a demonstrative sequence is a noun phrase or a complete sentence, which is the single most consequential decision this construction forces.

instructional_purpose: Presents a working set of governing particles that place their complement in the genitive, and shows that each one carries a spread of relational senses beyond its primary meaning. It also introduces verb-specific particle selection.
concepts_taught: a core set of genitive-governing particles
uniform genitive government over the following nominal
primary spatial or relational sense of each particle
extended and non-spatial senses of the same particle
paired particles marking a source-to-goal span
particles that are written joined to the following word
obligation and benefactive senses carried by particles
verb-specific particle selection

linguistic_propositions.proposition: Every member of this particle class places the nominal that follows it in the genitive.
A single particle covers several distinct relations, and the intended relation is fixed by context rather than by the particle alone.
Two of the particles are orthographically bound to the following word rather than written separately.
Some verbs select a specific particle, so the pairing is lexical rather than derivable from the particle's core sense.

The genitive is repeatedly identified with a kasra ending, while one illustration in the same lesson shows a genitive complement carrying a fatḥa; the diptote condition that explains this is never stated, leaving the two claims in tension inside the lesson.
The class is presented as having seven core members; the traditional inventory is considerably larger, and the lesson does not signal that it is a selection.

Words expressing location that also appear in the reading material are handled alongside these particles even though the standard classification treats them as adverbials rather than as members of this particle class.
The comparative use of the source particle is presented as one of its extended senses without distinguishing it from its origin sense on any formal criterion.

recognition_criteria: a closed-class function word immediately preceding a nominal
the following nominal shows a genitive marker, or would if it were fully vowelled
two members appear as a bound prefix on the following word rather than as separate tokens
the presence of a particular verb earlier in the clause can predict which particle appears
procedures: identify the particle
identify the nominal it governs
mark that nominal genitive
choose among the particle's senses using the surrounding verb and the semantics of the complement
when producing text, look up whether the governing verb lexically selects a particular particle rather than reasoning from the particle's core sense
for the two bound members, attach them orthographically and adjust for the definite article where required
conditions: genitive marking applies to whatever nominal directly follows the particle
the source-to-goal reading requires the paired particles to occur together in one clause
the bound members require orthographic attachment to the following word
exceptions: the surface marker of the genitive is not always the expected short vowel, as one of the lesson's own examples shows
the extended senses of a particle can be far from its spatial core, for example obligation or comparison
contrasts: source particle versus topic particle, which the lesson treats as a primary confusion pair
spatial sense versus abstract sense of the same particle
separately written particles versus orthographically bound particles
particle chosen by the speaker's meaning versus particle imposed by the governing verb

common_mistakes.pattern: leaving the complement of a particle in a non-genitive form
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the particle's defining property is that it imposes the genitive, so any other ending contradicts the government relation
common_mistakes.correction_principle: government by the particle overrides whatever ending the nominal would otherwise carry

common_mistakes.pattern: substituting the source particle for the topic particle or the reverse
common_mistakes.why_wrong: one introduces an origin or starting point and the other introduces subject matter, so the swap changes what the clause is about
common_mistakes.correction_principle: decide first whether the complement is an origin or a topic, then select accordingly

common_mistakes.pattern: pairing a verb with a particle chosen on general semantic grounds instead of the one it lexically selects
common_mistakes.why_wrong: particle selection with these verbs is idiomatic, so a semantically plausible substitute is still ungrammatical
common_mistakes.correction_principle: treat verb plus particle as a stored lexical pairing

misleading_shortcuts: equating the genitive with a kasra ending in all cases, which the lesson's own diptote example quietly falsifies
assuming one particle equals one English preposition
assuming the seven presented members are the whole class
assuming a particle's sense can always be predicted from its spatial core
worked_analysis_stages: locate the particle
identify its complement
assign the genitive
select the contextual sense from the particle's inventory of relations
paradigms: a particle-by-primary-sense table with one illustration per particle
per-particle sense tables listing extended relations alongside the core spatial one
exercise_types: multiple-choice case identification
multiple-choice sense identification for a given particle
fill-in series selecting the particle that fits a described relation
short translation into Arabic
end-of-lesson quiz combining case, sense and verb-particle pairing
prerequisite_knowledge: the three case labels and their markers
the definite article and how it merges with bound prefixes
basic noun and verb vocabulary
annexation, which produces a comparable genitive
reuses_from_earlier: attached pronouns as complements of these particles, from L1.M5.02
new_knowledge: the genitive-governing particle class as a class
multi-sense mapping for individual particles
paired particles for spans
verb-specific particle selection as a lexical fact
later_dependencies: annexation chains and complex noun phrases
clause-level scope and attachment decisions for prepositional phrases
sarf_relevance: low — the members are invariant function words, though the bound ones create a segmentation task
nahw_relevance: high — government, case assignment and phrase attachment are the whole content of the lesson
tutor_drill_relevance: high — case assignment is mechanical; sense selection and verb pairing need contextual items rather than isolated forms
rich_hover_relevance: high — a hover must give the particle's sense in this clause, not just a default gloss, and must mark the complement as governed
corpus_pvn_relevance: p-kind entries for each particle, each needing multiple sense entries rather than a single gloss; n-kind entries are affected downstream because governed nominals need a genitive reading; a per-verb pairing table would sit with v-kind entries

uncertainty_flags: internal tension between the general claim that the genitive shows as a kasra and an example where it does not
classification of location words as particles versus adverbials is analysis-dependent
the presented inventory is a pedagogical selection, not the full class

proposed_new_units.summary: A lexical licensing table pairing verbs with the genitive-governing particle they select, so that a sense-and-attachment decision can be made from the verb rather than from the particle's default gloss.
proposed_new_units.why_existing_insufficient: u-n03 encodes government abstractly and u-n07 covers particles with several functions, but neither stores the per-verb selection facts that decide which particle is grammatical and what relation it then expresses; without that table the multi-sense particle entries have no way to be narrowed at an occurrence.

instructional_purpose: Teaches the two ways Arabic forms questions, separating the particles that request a yes-or-no judgement from the words that request a specific piece of information, and assigns each interrogative word a syntactic slot.
concepts_taught: polar question particles
information-seeking interrogative words
the rational versus non-rational split between two interrogative words
interrogative words for place, time, manner and reason
the quantity interrogative and the form of the noun it counts
clause-initial placement of interrogatives
invariant interrogatives holding positional case
one declinable interrogative as the exception

linguistic_propositions.proposition: Two distinct particles introduce polar questions, and they occupy the front of the clause.
Interrogative words are almost all invariant in form yet occupy case-bearing slots, so they receive a positional case according to their function.
One interrogative asks about rational referents and another asks about non-rational ones; a related form is preferred immediately before a verb.
One interrogative in the class inflects for case and is therefore the exception to the invariance generalisation.

The quantity interrogative is said to require a singular accusative counted noun; that holds for the interrogative use only, and the interrogative itself takes a different pattern when it is governed by a particle, neither of which the lesson notes.

The lesson maps polar questions onto one classical question-type label and information questions onto another; in the traditional scheme one of the two polar particles serves both types, so the mapping is looser than presented.
Interrogative words are said to stand at the beginning of the sentence, yet the lesson's own positional-case illustration shows an interrogative preceded by a governing particle.
One of the two polar particles is characterised as belonging to a more formal or classical register.

recognition_criteria: a clause-initial closed-class word with no lexical content of its own signals a question
polar particles are followed by an otherwise complete clause
information interrogatives leave a gap corresponding to the requested constituent
an interrogative preceded by a governing particle is still the interrogative of its clause, merely carried along by the particle
a counted noun immediately after the quantity interrogative appears singular and accusative
procedures: decide whether the question requests a truth judgement or a specific constituent
for polar questions, place the particle at the front and leave the clause otherwise intact
for information questions, choose the interrogative matching the requested category (person, thing, place, time, manner, reason, quantity)
place the interrogative at the front, carrying any governing particle with it
assign the interrogative its positional case from the slot it corresponds to
for the quantity interrogative, put the counted noun in the required singular form
conditions: rational reference conditions the choice between the two who/what interrogatives
the verb-adjacent variant of the what-interrogative is preferred before verbs
the singular accusative counted noun applies to the interrogative quantity use
exceptions: one interrogative in the class inflects rather than staying invariant
an interrogative can be preceded by a governing particle, which qualifies the clause-initial rule
contrasts: polar particle versus information interrogative
rational versus non-rational interrogative
invariant interrogatives versus the one declinable member
the two polar particles distinguished by register
quantity interrogative versus ordinary numeral constructions

common_mistakes.pattern: placing a question particle somewhere other than the front of the clause
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the particle's function is to scope over the whole clause, so a medial position leaves the clause without a question operator in scope
common_mistakes.correction_principle: question operators take clause-initial position and scope rightward

common_mistakes.pattern: using the non-rational interrogative to ask about a person
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the rational/non-rational split is grammaticalised in this pair, so the wrong member misidentifies the class of the sought referent
common_mistakes.correction_principle: select the interrogative by the rationality of the expected answer

common_mistakes.pattern: putting a plural noun after the quantity interrogative
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the counted element in this construction takes a singular form, so a plural breaks the required pattern
common_mistakes.correction_principle: the quantity interrogative imposes a fixed shape on the counted noun rather than agreeing with the intended plural sense

misleading_shortcuts: taking 'interrogatives always come first' as absolute, which the lesson's own governed example contradicts
treating the two polar particles as freely interchangeable
generalising the singular accusative rule to every use of the quantity word
treating all interrogatives as invariant and so failing to inflect the one that does

name the positional case implied by the slot
name the function label for that slot

instructional_purpose: Shows that Arabic expresses possession without any verb corresponding to 'have', using a fronted adverbial or particle phrase as the predicate with the possessed item as a delayed subject, and distinguishes the available exponents by nuance and register.
concepts_taught: absence of a dedicated possession verb
fronted predicate with a delayed subject as the possession frame

a formal or literary alternant for the availability sense
an accompaniment expression that can imply possession
nominative marking on the possessed item
negation of the possession frame

linguistic_propositions.proposition: Possession is expressed by a predication frame rather than by a transitive verb, so no direct object is ever involved.
In this frame the possessed item is the subject and the location or benefactive phrase is the fronted predicate, which is why the possessed item is nominative.
Different exponents carry different nuances: one leans toward availability or physical presence, another toward ownership or entitlement.
One exponent is described as belonging to formal or written register rather than differing in meaning.

The lesson groups the location words used here with the genitive-governing particles under a single heading; in the standard classification those location words are adverbials of place taking the accusative, not members of the particle class.
Negation is introduced with two operators, one of which behaves differently across the grammatical schools when it negates a verbless sentence.
The nuance table between the availability exponent and the ownership exponent is a usage tendency, not a rule that decides any given occurrence.
An indefinite item appears as the subject here, which is licensed precisely because the predicate is fronted; the lesson states the resulting case but not the licensing condition.

recognition_criteria: there is no verb in the clause, yet a possession relation is asserted
a location or benefactive phrase carrying a person suffix stands first
the item said to be possessed follows and is nominative, commonly indefinite
a negating operator before the fronted phrase signals denial of possession rather than negation of any verb
procedures: choose the exponent by whether availability, ownership, accompaniment or formal register is intended
attach the appropriate person suffix to that exponent
place the resulting phrase first
place the possessed item after it in the nominative
to negate, prefix the appropriate negating operator while keeping the possessed item nominative
conditions: the possessed item stays nominative because it is the subject, not a complement
an indefinite subject is acceptable here only because the predicate has been fronted
the person suffix must be the attached series, since these hosts do not take free pronouns
exceptions: the accompaniment expression only implies possession in some contexts rather than asserting it
the choice between availability and ownership exponents is defeasible, so context can override the default nuance
contrasts: availability exponent versus ownership exponent
neutral register versus formal or literary alternant
possession framing versus an ordinary transitive clause with a direct object
affirmative frame versus its two negated variants

common_mistakes.pattern: treating the availability and ownership exponents as interchangeable
common_mistakes.why_wrong: they differ in whether they assert access or title, so substituting one for the other shifts what is being claimed
common_mistakes.correction_principle: select the exponent from the intended relation, then check the context does not override it

common_mistakes.pattern: combining these hosts with a free pronoun instead of an attached one
common_mistakes.why_wrong: these hosts require the attached series, so a free pronoun leaves them without a licensed complement
common_mistakes.correction_principle: apply the series-selection rule from the attached pronoun lesson

common_mistakes.pattern: marking the possessed item accusative as though it were an object

common_mistakes.correction_principle: identify the frame before assigning case: no verb means no object slot

instructional_purpose: Teaches the negator that leaves an imperfect verb in its default mood, contrasts it with the other negating operators by tense and by mood effect, and separates it from the identically written prohibitive.
concepts_taught: negating an imperfect verb without altering its mood

linguistic_propositions.proposition: This negator leaves the imperfect verb in its default mood, unlike the operators that impose the two dependent moods.
The same written shape functions both as a negator of statements and as a prohibitive, and only the verb's mood distinguishes the two.
Two other operators take the imperfect form but shift the time reference, one to the past and one to the future, and each imposes a distinct mood.
The comparison table assigns one operator to the perfect form and past time only; that operator also negates the imperfect and verbless sentences, which the table does not show.
The negator that operates on verbless sentences is listed in the table but its own government effects are not taught here.
The use of this shape as a categorical negator of a whole class, which imposes a different case on the following noun, is absent from the lesson although it shares the same written form.
Mood is presented as a diagnostic that reliably separates the negative from the prohibitive; in unvocalised text that diagnostic is frequently unavailable.

recognition_criteria: the negator stands immediately before an imperfect verb
the verb keeps its default mood ending, which is the signal that this is the statement negator
a dependent mood ending on the following verb signals the prohibitive reading instead
the negator standing alone with no following verb is a bare answer
several high-frequency fixed expressions consist of the negator plus a single following word
procedures: decide the time reference and the form of the verb to be negated
select the operator that matches that combination
place the operator immediately before the verb
for this negator, leave the verb's mood untouched
to distinguish statement negation from prohibition, inspect the mood of the verb rather than the negator
conditions: default mood retention is specific to this negator
the past and future negators require their respective dependent moods on the verb

exceptions: the same written shape has a prohibitive function that behaves differently

contrasts: statement negator versus prohibitive, distinguished only by the verb's mood
this negator versus the past negator versus the future negator, by mood and time reference
negation of a verb versus negation of a verbless sentence

instructional_purpose: Orients the learner to the coexistence of a standardised written variety and regional spoken varieties, explains why the course teaches the standard variety first, and sets expectations about variation. It teaches no new grammatical rule.
concepts_taught: the standard variety and its domains of use

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The language community operates with two functionally separated varieties, distributed by domain rather than by speaker competence.
Case endings are systematically realised in the standard variety and generally absent in the spoken varieties.
Regional varieties differ in vocabulary, in pronunciation of particular consonants, and in some grammatical exponents.
Switching between varieties according to situation is ordinary competence, not deficiency.
The lesson uses one label to cover both the classical language and the modern standardised written language, which collapses a distinction that matters for any corpus that spans both.

Regional varieties are said not to be reliably mutually intelligible, while the standard variety is said to be understood by educated speakers across regions; both are sociolinguistic generalisations admitting many exceptions.
The claim that one particular regional variety is broadly understood because of media reach is a sociolinguistic observation, not a grammatical fact, and is stated without qualification.

Learning the standard variety first is presented as the correct sequencing because it underlies the others; the framing of dialects as variations built on the standard is a pedagogical stance rather than a historical claim the lesson defends.

nahw_relevance: low — the only syntactic point is the observation that case endings are typically absent in spoken varieties, which is stated rather than analysed
tutor_drill_relevance: low — the content is orientation and terminology; the only checkable items are definitions and domain matching
